First, for the purposes of this study, the authors are hypothesizing a scenario of hull- integration with a new facility, whereby aspects of OTEC integration can be considered during the facility’s design phase. This choice was made based on the understanding and consensus of the consulted entities that retrofitting an existing facility with hull-integrated OTEC would be cost-prohibitive. Additionally, while existing offshore oil and gas facilities in the GOA are considered in this study, they are included as hypothetical scenarios. It is understood that the existing oil and gas facilities have highly variable remaining service life, and they may not be viable candidates for adding OTEC. Stakeholder decisions for OTEC integration of any configuration must take into account location-specific realities, such as regulatory restrictions, structural possibilities, service life, and economic feasibility. The real LCOE calculation shows the theoretical opportunity of OTEC-produced power. While the authors have made every effort to document the individual costs comprising the hypothetical integration of an OTEC plant with an oil and gas facility, it is advisable that stakeholders treat the model presented here as a tool to quickly assess theoretical possibilities and not economic feasibility. One of the major limitations contributing to the highly hypothetical nature of this study is the limited OTEC operation experience in the U.S. and globally. This limited experience drives the admittedly limited understanding of OTEC operation and maintenance costs—especially in a new setting, such as coupled to a GOA oil and gas facility. Other factors, including hydrodynamics, while studied in referenced literature documented in the Objective 2 report, are also hypothetical. 7 Key Insights and Remaining Uncertainties This study has led to key insights with regard to the hypothetical possibility of OTEC deployment in the GOA. At the same time, uncertainties and knowledge gaps still exist. The insights gained from this study are summarized below, in no particular order. • For peak efficiency, an oil and gas facility-coupled OTEC plant must be designed such that the key equipment is within 30 feet above sea level. • The relatively large seasonal variation of surface water temperatures in the U.S. Gulf of America waters is one of the key deterrents from OTEC being considered as a viable large-scale power generation choice.
